definition: A feeling of fear or anxiety about something that may happen.
exampleSentence: She opened the results with trepidation.
etymology: From Latin 'trepidare' meaning to tremble or hurry with alarm.

definition: Great happiness and exhilaration.
exampleSentence: A wave of elation swept over the crowd at the final whistle.
etymology: From Latin 'elatus' meaning raised or lifted up.

definition: The feeling that someone is beneath consideration or worthless.
exampleSentence: She looked at the cheat with open contempt.
etymology: From Latin 'contemnere' meaning to despise or scorn.

definition: Deep regret or guilt for a wrong committed.
exampleSentence: He showed no remorse for the damage he'd caused.
etymology: From Latin 'remordere' meaning to bite back — guilt that gnaws.

definition: A feeling of intense irritation or frustration.
exampleSentence: She sighed in exasperation at the endless delays.
etymology: From Latin 'exasperare' meaning to roughen or irritate — from 'asper' (rough).

definition: A feeling that something bad is about to happen.
exampleSentence: A sense of foreboding filled the silent house.
etymology: From 'fore-' (before) + 'bode' (to portend), from Old English 'bodian' (to announce).

definition: A deep, often wistful longing.
exampleSentence: She felt a yearning for the city she'd left behind.
etymology: From Old English 'giernan' meaning to desire eagerly.

definition: The release of strong emotions, bringing relief.
exampleSentence: Writing about the loss was a kind of catharsis.
etymology: From Greek 'katharsis' meaning a cleansing — used by Aristotle for drama's effect.

definition: The power of making one's own choices or decisions.
exampleSentence: She left of her own volition, with no pressure from anyone.
etymology: From Latin 'volo' meaning I wish or I will.

definition: A person's nature regarding how they typically behave and feel.
exampleSentence: Her calm temperament suits high-pressure work.
etymology: From Latin 'temperamentum' meaning a proper mixture — of the four humors.

definition: A person's inherent qualities of mind and character.
exampleSentence: He has a cheerful disposition that brightens the room.
etymology: From Latin 'dispositio' meaning arrangement — from 'disponere' (to arrange).

definition: A feeling that makes one self-conscious and unable to act freely.
exampleSentence: After a while she lost her inhibitions and danced.
etymology: From Latin 'inhibere' meaning to hold in — 'in' + 'habere' (to hold).

definition: An irresistible urge to behave in a certain way.
exampleSentence: He felt a compulsion to check the lock twice.
etymology: From Latin 'compellere' meaning to drive together or force.

definition: Showing great attention to detail; very careful.
exampleSentence: Her meticulous notes made the report easy to follow.
etymology: From Latin 'meticulosus' meaning fearful — later shifted to overly careful.

definition: Showing a willingness to take bold risks.
exampleSentence: It was an audacious plan that just might work.
etymology: From Latin 'audax' meaning bold — from 'audere' (to dare).

definition: Wishing to do one's work thoroughly and well.
exampleSentence: A conscientious employee, she never cut corners.
etymology: From Latin 'conscientia' meaning knowledge within oneself, i.e. conscience.

definition: Wanting to avoid activity or effort; lazy.
exampleSentence: He spent an indolent afternoon in the hammock.
etymology: From Latin 'indolens' meaning painless — 'in-' (not) + 'dolere' (to feel pain).

definition: Careful and economical with money or resources.
exampleSentence: Her frugal habits let her save half her income.
etymology: From Latin 'frugalis' meaning useful or worthy — from 'frux' (fruit, profit).

definition: Bold and without shame.
exampleSentence: It was a brazen lie told to everyone's face.
etymology: From Old English 'bræsen' meaning made of brass — figuratively hard-faced.

definition: Severe or strict in manner; plain and without comfort.
exampleSentence: The monastery's austere rooms held only a bed and a candle.
etymology: From Greek 'austeros' meaning harsh or bitter to the taste.

definition: Diligent and thorough, with careful attention to what is right.
exampleSentence: She was scrupulous about returning every borrowed cent.
etymology: From Latin 'scrupulus' meaning a small sharp stone — a tiny worry in the mind.

definition: The quality of being open and honest.
exampleSentence: I appreciated her candor about the risks.
etymology: From Latin 'candor' meaning brightness or whiteness — purity of speech.

definition: Showing sensitivity in dealing with others or difficult issues.
exampleSentence: She gave a tactful answer that hurt no one.
etymology: From 'tact' (Latin 'tactus', touch) + '-ful' — a delicate touch in dealings.

definition: A person who helps another commit a crime or wrongdoing.
exampleSentence: The thief had an accomplice waiting in the car.
etymology: From Old French 'complice' (associate), reshaped under 'accompany'.

definition: A person who gives money or help to a person or cause.
exampleSentence: An anonymous benefactor paid for the new library.
etymology: From Latin 'bene' (well) + 'facere' (to do) — one who does good.

definition: A person who supports an artist, cause, or establishment.
exampleSentence: The duke was a famous patron of painters.
etymology: From Latin 'patronus' meaning protector — from 'pater' (father).

definition: A person who is responsible for looking after something.
exampleSentence: Museums act as custodians of our shared heritage.
etymology: From Latin 'custos' meaning guard or keeper.

definition: A person sent on a special mission as a representative.
exampleSentence: An emissary was sent to negotiate the ceasefire.
etymology: From Latin 'emissarius' meaning one sent out — from 'emittere' (to send out).

definition: A person or thing that follows and takes the place of another.
exampleSentence: She named her successor before retiring.
etymology: From Latin 'succedere' meaning to come after — 'sub' + 'cedere' (to go).

definition: To express sharp disapproval or criticism.
exampleSentence: The coach rebuked the players for their laziness.
etymology: From Old French 'rebuker' meaning to beat back.

definition: To suggest something unpleasant in an indirect way.
exampleSentence: Are you insinuating that I lied?
etymology: From Latin 'insinuare' meaning to wind one's way in — from 'sinus' (curve).

definition: To turn aside from the main subject in speech or writing.
exampleSentence: Sorry, I digress — let me return to the point.
etymology: From Latin 'digressus' meaning a going apart — 'dis' + 'gradi' (to step).

definition: To admit something is true, often reluctantly; to surrender.
exampleSentence: He conceded that she had a point.
etymology: From Latin 'concedere' meaning to yield — 'con' + 'cedere' (to go, withdraw).

definition: To express grief or deep regret about something.
exampleSentence: Critics lament the loss of the old theater.
etymology: From Latin 'lamentari' meaning to wail or weep.

definition: To rebuke or scold severely.
exampleSentence: The teacher chastised them for arriving late.
etymology: From Latin 'castigare' meaning to correct or purify.

definition: To state again strongly one's support or belief.
exampleSentence: The leaders reaffirmed their commitment to peace.
etymology: From 're-' (again) + 'affirm', from Latin 'affirmare' (to make firm).

definition: A lack of energy and enthusiasm; sluggishness.
exampleSentence: A wave of lethargy hit her after the heavy lunch.
etymology: From Greek 'lethargia' — related to 'lethe' (forgetfulness).

definition: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands.
exampleSentence: Playing the violin demands great dexterity.
etymology: From Latin 'dexteritas' meaning readiness — from 'dexter' (right-handed, skillful).

definition: To suddenly move back in fear or disgust.
exampleSentence: She recoiled at the sight of the spider.
etymology: From Old French 'reculer' meaning to move back — from 'cul' (rear).

definition: Sleep, especially of a light or peaceful kind.
exampleSentence: The baby fell into a deep slumber.
etymology: From Middle English 'slumeren', from Old English 'sluma' (light sleep).

definition: To recover one's health gradually after illness.
exampleSentence: She went to the coast to convalesce after surgery.
etymology: From Latin 'convalescere' — 'con' + 'valescere' (to grow strong).

definition: To soak food in a seasoned liquid before cooking.
exampleSentence: Marinate the chicken overnight for the best flavor.
etymology: From French 'mariner' meaning to pickle in brine — from 'marin' (of the sea).

definition: To undergo a chemical change caused by microorganisms.
exampleSentence: Grapes are left to ferment into wine.
etymology: From Latin 'fermentum' meaning leaven — from 'fervere' (to boil).

definition: To decorate food with small extra items.
exampleSentence: Garnish the soup with fresh basil.
etymology: From Old French 'garnir' meaning to equip or adorn.

definition: Great enthusiasm; also the outer peel of a citrus fruit.
exampleSentence: She approached every task with zest.
etymology: From French 'zeste' meaning orange or lemon peel.

definition: To reach the highest or final point.
exampleSentence: Years of work culminated in a single triumphant night.
etymology: From Latin 'culmen' meaning summit or peak.

definition: To gradually diminish in size, amount, or strength.
exampleSentence: Their savings dwindled over the long winter.
etymology: From Old English 'dwinan' meaning to waste away.

definition: To spread throughout something.
exampleSentence: The smell of coffee permeated the whole house.
etymology: From Latin 'permeare' meaning to pass through — 'per' + 'meare' (to go).

definition: To voluntarily give up a possession, right, or claim.
exampleSentence: He refused to relinquish control of the company.
etymology: From Latin 'relinquere' meaning to leave behind — 're' + 'linquere' (to leave).

definition: To grow or develop rapidly.
exampleSentence: The city's tech sector began to burgeon.
etymology: From Old French 'burjon' meaning a bud or shoot.
